sources.title: Cyril Toumanoff, Bagratids, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Directly read. Use chronology and institutions, not the article’s moral judgments about dynastic failure. Armenian kingship restored in the 880s; Ani annexed in 1045.

sources.title: Robert H. Hewsen, Ayrarat, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Directly read. Historical geography, capitals, Byzantine annexation, Seljuk conquest, Georgian and Mongol domination. Approximate political transitions are not exact map-boundary dates.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Site of Ani
sources.note: Directly read, especially Outstanding Universal Value and brief synthesis. Multi-period buildings; slow decline and eventual near-abandonment, not instantaneous disappearance in 1319.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Armenia! Exhibition Galleries (2018)
sources.note: Directly read. Architecture, Cilicia and Greater Armenia scriptoria. Some manuscript examples extend into the fourteenth century and later; public text explicitly marks broad medieval practices rather than claiming every illustration predates 1279.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Monasteries of Haghpat and Sanahin
sources.note: Original institutional indexed text checked; slash-ending direct request returned 503. Tenth- to thirteenth-century foundations, learning and Sanahin calligraphers.

sources.title: Republic of Armenia, Haghpat and Sanahin Monasteries management plan, hosted by UNESCO
sources.note: Original indexed PDF text, printed p.197, Scriptorium and Seminary of Grigor Magistros. Direct web fetch failed. Named patron Hranush, 1063 construction and wall niches directly supported.

sources.title: Kh. Grigoryan and L. Aleksanyan, Lore Fortress: Large City (2019)
sources.note: Published by Service for the Protection of Historical Environment and Cultural Museum-Reservations, SNCO, Hayrapet, Yerevan. Full 50-page PDF downloaded and text read locally. Human PDF pages 28 to 33 describe medieval bathhouses.

sources.title: Kate Franklin, Everyday Cosmopolitanisms: Living the Silk Road in Medieval Armenia (University of California Press, 2021)
sources.note: Full open-access primary archaeological monograph downloaded and read. Printed pp.103 to 105 and 116 to 121; Arai-Bazarjul caravanserai and Ambroyi contexts are thirteenth to fourteenth century, not confined to pre-1279. All uses of this book share one word budget.

sources.title: Research on Armenian Architecture, Dadivank hall inscription, 1211 (Armenian transcription)
sources.note: Directly read six-line transcription. Final word ՅԻՇԵՑԷՔ is represented in modern type, not a facsimile. English counterpart supplies published translation; both pages treated as one work.

sources.title: Research on Armenian Architecture, Dadivank hall inscription, 1211 (English translation)
sources.note: Directly read translation and architectural description. Count jointly with Armenian counterpart. Source’s modern territorial labels are not adopted as sovereignty claims.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Distinct highland regional narrative, not a continuous Bagratid state and not Cilician Armenia. Keep imported 1000 to 1279 interval and explain omitted 1100 to 1200 snapshot. Replace erroneous Sasanian E alias.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Identical highland outline at 1000 to 1100 and 1200 to 1279; bbox 41.006,36.782,46.907,41.458. Does not reach Sis/Cilicia. See ../identities.json.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: 1211 Dadivank princely hall inscription, not the cathedral inscription of 1214. Armenian modern transcription and English translation checked directly. Translation of one word is secure; no facsimile claim.
batchIdentityNotes.budget: Armenian and English RAA monument pages count as one underlying work. Franklin book uses count jointly; its thirteenth- to fourteenth-century evidence is explicitly dated in each standalone passage.
